channel.title: From highschool math to university statistics
channel.description: A blog for university students about statistics

item.title: Part 1 - Why statistics?
item.dc:creator: Job Oussoren
item.description:
Welcome to the blog! My name is Job (24) and I’m a Master student in the program: Child Development and Education. I don’t have the years of statistical experience your statistics professors have so I’m not a seasoned mathematician or statistician. But, I am, like you, growing up in a word of AI, social media and massive computing power. With this blog I hope to provide a place where conceptual thinking, intuition (or the lack of it) and statistics come together. Together I hope to explore how statistics can be less about equations, rules and R-code, and more about order, disorder and beauty. Furthermore I hope to connect math concepts from highschool to university statistics concepts to illustrate that most of already know a lot about stats, we just have to get used to the terminology. I aim to do this because I experienced a lack of connection between highschool math and bachelor statistics when I started with my bachelor “Pedagogical Sciences”. Lastly, because my area of interest is child, development and education, most of this blog will revolve around these topics.

Why would we do statistics?

In my second year of my bachelors one of the ethics professors made us read the paper The Lure of Statistics for Educational Researchers by David Labaree. Labaree learned me that quantifying can be a coping mechanism for how weak the soft sciences (e.g., child, development and education) are when measuring behavior. For example, a physics or chemistry scientist can rely on a themometer for measuring temperature, soft sciences researches do not have such a instrument for quantifying (complex) behavior. Labaree states that this notion makes us seek statistics as a way to compensate for this weakness. Furthermore, researchers in the soft sciences generally experience a pressure to quantify their findings as a warrant for funding and being accepted to prestigious journals.

So, I start with a wake-up call. Statistics can be fuzzy and very complex, which can hinder interpretability. Statistics can be used to manipulate data to get made up results which can foster bad science. But statistics can be also very elegant and intuitive. Feeling this elegance of statistics is a feeling best expressed in the scene “Can you hear the music” from the Oppenheimer movie.

And that is what I want to experience together. I want to recreate the feeling when you first learned to bike. Or the feeling when you first solved that difficult equation in highschool. All these events where you “heard the music”, I hope you will also start “hearing the music” when doing statistics together.
